summary: Describes the format for exchanging Network News articles among USENET sites, with only partial standards for transmission. It was circulated for information and does not specify an Internet standard. Replaced by RFC 1036.

eli5.summary: The rules for how online discussion posts are written so different sites can share them.

subtitle: The standard format for Network News articles shared among USENET sites.

tldr.problem: USENET sites need a standard format for exchanging news articles so implementations can interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Articles are formatted as valid RFC 822 mail messages with required headers (From, Date, Subject, Message-ID, Newsgroups, Path) and optional headers, followed by article body. Control messages enable network administration.
tldr.outcome: USENET used this standard for networked discussions; it was later superseded by RFC 1036.

facts.label: Required headers
facts.value: 8: Relay-Version, Posting-Version, From, Date, Newsgroups, Subject, Message-ID, Path

facts.label: Control message encapsulation
facts.value: Each line prefixed with N for mail transmission

today: RFC 850 is the original USENET standard but is now informational. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1036.

sections.title: USENET and Article Distribution
sections.content:
This RFC defines the standard format for Network News articles shared among USENET sites. USENET is a logical network built on top of physical networks like UUCP, ARPANET, and Ethernet, not a single standardized network. Articles are formatted as valid RFC 822 mail messages to leverage existing mail tools, but with stricter rules and extensions specific to news.

The RFC covers the article format, valid control messages for network administration, transmission methods (remote execution, mail, batching), and the overall news propagation algorithm. Transmission is only partially standardized to allow flexibility in hardware and software choices.
sections.eli5: USENET is news groups spread across different computers. This memo says how to write news messages so they work everywhere, using the same rules as email but stricter.

sections.title: Article Headers and Structure
sections.content:
An article consists of header lines followed by a blank line and the article body. Each header is keyword: value. Required headers are: Relay-Version (identifies the relay program), Posting-Version (identifies software that posted the article), From (mailing address and optional full name), Date (original posting time), Newsgroups (comma-separated list of newsgroup names), Subject, Message-ID (unique identifier), and Path (route the article took through the network).

Message-ID format is <unique@domain> and must not be reused for at least two years. Path accumulates site names as the article propagates, enabling loop detection and preventing redundant delivery. The From line supports three formats: plain address, address with full name in parentheses, or full name with address in angle brackets.
sections.eli5: News messages need headers like email: who wrote it, when, what group it is for, and a unique number so no two messages are the same. The Path shows which computers the message passed through.

sections.title: Optional Headers and Fields
sections.content:
Optional headers include Reply-To (alternative reply address), Sender (submitter, when different from author), Followup-To (redirect followups to a different newsgroup), Date-Received (local receipt time, replaced on relay), Expires (suggested expiration date for cleanup), References (message IDs of parent articles, required for followups), Control (marks article as a control message for hosts, not users), Distribution (restricts delivery to a subset of sites), and Organization (identifies the sender's organization).

References chains articles into threaded conversations. A followup includes the parent's References and appends the parent's Message-ID. Distribution uses the same format as Newsgroups and allows wildcards, restricting distribution scope. Unrecognized headers are passed through unchanged.
sections.eli5: Optional headers let you say who should read it (Distribution), what group to reply in (Followup-To), when to throw it away (Expires), and which message you are replying to (References).

sections.title: Control Messages for Network Administration
sections.content:
Control messages are articles with a Control header, processed by hosts rather than shown to users. Valid control messages include cancel <message-id> (author or superuser deletes an article), ihave/sendme (negotiate article exchange to reduce redundant traffic), newgroup <groupname> (create a newsgroup), rmgroup <groupname> (remove a newsgroup), sendsys (request the neighbor configuration), senduuname (request UUCP neighbors), and version (request software name and version).

Sites may handle control messages automatically or queue them for manual processing. Cancel requires verification that the requester is the original author. Ihave/sendme allows sites to negotiate which articles to send, reducing bandwidth. Sendsys responses describe the site's neighbors and which newsgroup patterns are sent to each.
sections.eli5: Special messages let computers talk to each other: deleting a message, creating a new discussion group, asking about neighbors, or saying what software they use.

sections.title: Transmission Methods and Propagation
sections.content:
Articles are transmitted via remote execution (spooling rnews on the remote system via UUCP or Berknet), mail (sending the article as mail body to user newsmail or encapsulated to user rnews, with each line prefixed by N), or batching (multiple articles in a script separated by #! rnews <size> headers). Batching saves transmission overhead but requires unbatching on receipt.

USENET propagates as a directed graph where each arc is labeled with newsgroup patterns. When an article is posted to a newsgroup, the originating site forwards it to all interested neighbors, who forward to their neighbors. Loop prevention uses a history mechanism tracking message IDs and the Path header: sites never resend articles they have already seen or send articles back to sites in the Path.
sections.eli5: Messages travel computer to computer, either run as a command, sent as mail, or bundled together. Each computer remembers which messages it has seen so they do not go in circles forever.

sections.title: Compatibility and Older Formats
sections.content:
The standard allows backward compatibility with older article formats. The older format used different header names (Title instead of Subject, Article-I.D. instead of Message-ID, Posted for date) and a compact A format with fields on separate lines. The new RFC 822-based format is preferred, but implementations should accept and convert older formats to ease migration.

Sites must maintain Path headers in a format suitable for reply routing until 1984 to support non-Internet mailers. Domain names in addresses are case-insensitive, but user names may not be; software should avoid changing case. Full names in From lines are restricted to printing ASCII excluding parentheses and angle brackets.
sections.eli5: Older computers used different rules, so new systems need to understand the old format and convert it. Site names do not care about capital letters, but user names might.
